name: Wireless & Cellular Security
description: Security of cellular (4G/5G), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, and other RF/wireless protocols.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list zero in on two themes that would recur for years: spoofing of physical-layer signals and the messy security of legacy interfaces. "All Your GPS Are Belong To Us: Towards Stealthy Manipulation of Road Navigation Systems" (USENIX 2018) showed that GPS spoofing could be made stealthy enough to quietly reroute drivers, while "ATtention Spanned: Comprehensive Vulnerability Analysis of AT Commands Within the Android Ecosystem" (USENIX 2018) revealed that 1980s-era modem commands still expose modern smartphones, and "Off-Path TCP Exploit: How Wireless Routers Can Jeopardize Your Secrets" (USENIX 2018) turned a Wi-Fi half-duplex timing side channel into a remote secret-stealing attack. Together they framed wireless security as a problem of trusting open mediums and inherited legacy protocols.

By 2019-2020 the field pivoted hard toward the cellular and short-range stacks. On LTE, "Hiding in Plain Signal: Physical Signal Overshadowing Attack on LTE" (USENIX 2019) demonstrated that an attacker could overshadow legitimate broadcasts, and "Call Me Maybe: Eavesdropping Encrypted LTE Calls With ReVoLTE" (USENIX 2020) broke voice confidentiality by exploiting keystream reuse. Bluetooth saw a parallel wave: "The KNOB is Broken: Exploiting Low Entropy in the Encryption Key Negotiation Of Bluetooth BR/EDR" (USENIX 2019) attacked the standard itself, while "Frankenstein: Advanced Wireless Fuzzing to Exploit New Bluetooth Escalation Targets" (USENIX 2020) brought systematic fuzzing to firmware. The period also broadened the attack surface to proprietary and vehicular wireless links, from "A Billion Open Interfaces for Eve and Mallory" (USENIX 2019) on Apple Wireless Direct Link to "Plug-N-Pwned" (USENIX 2020) on automotive OBD-II dongles.

From 2021 onward the work matured from one-off exploits toward privacy attacks, defenses, and automated, specification-grounded analysis. Side channels grew subtler, with "A Stealthy Location Identification Attack Exploiting Carrier Aggregation in Cellular Networks" (USENIX 2021) and "Watching the Watchers: Practical Video Identification Attack in LTE Networks" (USENIX 2022) inferring location and even streamed video from encrypted traffic. Defenders answered with practical countermeasures like "Stars Can Tell: A Robust Method to Defend against GPS Spoofing Attacks using Off-the-shelf Chipset" (USENIX 2021) and protocol fixes such as "Privacy-Preserving and Standard-Compatible AKA Protocol for 5G" (USENIX 2021) and "Formal Analysis and Patching of BLE-SC Pairing" (USENIX 2023).

The most recent thread is scale: rather than hunting bugs by hand, researchers now reason over standards and baseband implementations automatically. "DoLTEst" (USENIX 2022) systematized negative testing of LTE devices, "Seeing the Forest for the Trees" (USENIX 2022) mined 3GPP change requests for spec-level hazards, "Sherlock on Specs" (USENIX 2023) and "BASECOMP" (USENIX 2023) tackled conformance testing and baseband integrity, and "Logic Gone Astray: A Security Analysis Framework for the Control Plane Protocols of 5G Basebands" (USENIX 2024) brought differential testing to 5G control-plane logic. The arc runs from clever physical-layer spoofs to automated, formal scrutiny of the cellular ecosystem itself.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection zeroes in on the mobile core: cellular authentication and location privacy. LTEInspector (NDSS 2018) introduced a systematic, model-based way to hunt for adversarial behavior in 4G LTE's attach, paging, and detach procedures, and GUTI Reallocation Demystified (NDSS 2018) showed that the very temporary identifiers meant to protect subscribers could be exploited for location tracking. Alongside this cellular focus, Device Pairing at the Touch of an Electrode (NDSS 2018) hints at the broader wireless-pairing thread that would grow in later years. Together these set the two enduring questions of the area: can we prove a protocol secure, and can an attacker quietly track or impersonate a device?

The next few years deepened both questions. Privacy Attacks to the 4G and 5G Cellular Paging Protocols (NDSS 2019) turned paging side channels into practical tracking, while Component-Based Formal Analysis of 5G-AKA (NDSS 2019) brought formal verification to the then-new 5G authentication standard and found channel and session-confusion issues before mass rollout. IMP4GT (NDSS 2020) landed a headline result by breaking LTE's assumed mutual authentication with real impersonation attacks. The community also began shifting from paper specifications to real implementations: BaseSpec (NDSS 2021) cross-checked baseband software against the standards, and FirmWire (NDSS 2022) made closed baseband firmware amenable to emulation and fuzzing. In parallel, defensive tooling emerged with PHOENIX (NDSS 2021) monitoring protocol behavior on the device itself.

At the same time the scope widened well beyond cellular into the full RF spectrum. Bluetooth and BLE became a sustained target, from BadBluetooth (NDSS 2019) through formal analysis of Bluetooth Passkey Entry pairing (NDSS 2023); GPS and drones drove SemperFi (NDSS 2022); Wi-Fi work spanned app fingerprinting (NDSS 2022), TCP hijacking in NAT-enabled Wi-Fi (NDSS 2024), and beamforming-feedback privacy leaks (NDSS 2025). Aviation and automotive RF also recur, from pilot reactions to avionic attacks (NDSS 2020) and ADS-B witnessing (NDSS 2021) to keyless-entry attacks on the Tesla Model 3 (NDSS 2023). By 2024-2025 the emphasis tilted toward defense and detection at scale, with 5G-Spector (NDSS 2024) offering O-RAN-compliant Layer-3 attack detection and IMSI-Catcher detection via identity-exposing messages (NDSS 2025).

The most recent NDSS 2026 papers show an area that is simultaneously maturing and expanding. Bluetooth/BLE pairing is under intense, formal scrutiny — BLERP: BLE Re-Pairing Attacks and Defenses, Formal Analysis of BLE Secure Connection Pairing and its PE Confusion Attack, and the context-aware fuzzer BSFuzzer all probe the same ubiquitous protocol from complementary angles. Cellular work continues to find concrete real-world exposure, from Passive Multi-Target GUTI Identification via Visual-RF Correlation to Small Cell, Big Risk's assessment of LTE femtocells in the wild and SIPConfusion's caller-ID and SMS spoofing. And the frontier keeps moving into new devices and cross-domain sensing: XR headsets leaking WiFi packets enable cross-building keylogging, WCDCAnalyzer scales Wi-Fi certified-connectivity analysis, and Unknown Target uncovers novel in-flight attacks on aircraft collision avoidance (TCAS) — evidence that "wireless and cellular security" now spans everything from the mobile core to Bluetooth, satellites, avionics, and emerging XR hardware.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this list treats wireless security as a set of physical-layer and signaling problems, each tied to a specific medium. On the location side, Crowd-GPS-Sec (S&P 2018) leaned on crowdsourced aircraft reports to detect and localize GPS spoofing against aviation, while Security of GPS/INS Based On-road Location Tracking Systems (S&P 2019) showed how fused GPS/inertial navigation could still be steered off course. In parallel, a device-pairing and distance-bounding thread emerged: Do You Feel What I Hear? (S&P 2018) and Secure Device Bootstrapping Without Secrets (S&P 2018) tackled how devices establish trust without prior secrets, and Sonar (S&P 2018) used audio-based distance bounding to catch SS7 call-redirection attacks in the telephony core.

The turn of the decade brought the cellular and short-range protocols themselves under formal scrutiny. Breaking LTE on Layer Two (S&P 2019) and Touching the Untouchables (S&P 2019) exposed data- and control-plane weaknesses in LTE, kicking off a durable line of protocol-analysis work. Bluetooth became a recurring target with BIAS: Bluetooth Impersonation AttackS (S&P 2020), full-band de-anonymization of Bluetooth Classic devices (S&P 2020), and the Method Confusion Attack on Bluetooth Pairing (S&P 2021), while Wi-Fi's WPA3 rollout was undercut almost immediately by Dragonblood (S&P 2020). A key methodological shift is visible here: rather than one-off exploits, researchers began building automated and formal tooling to find flaws at scale, as in Bookworm Game's documentation-driven LTE vulnerability discovery (S&P 2021) and, soon after, Formal Model-Driven Discovery of Bluetooth Protocol Design Vulnerabilities (S&P 2022) and BLEDiff (S&P 2023).

By the mid-2020s the field broadened along two axes. First, the attack surface expanded outward to new physical domains and cross-layer effects: maritime VSAT links (A Tale of Sea and Sky, S&P 2020), satellites (Space Odyssey, S&P 2023), mmWave radar sensing and spoofing (mmSpy, S&P 2022; mmEcho and mmSpoof, S&P 2023), and even inter-chip privilege escalation via wireless coexistence (S&P 2022). Second, privacy and sensing moved to center stage, with physical-layer BLE location tracking (S&P 2022) and its countermeasures (IRShield, S&P 2022; Practical Obfuscation of BLE Physical-Layer Fingerprints, S&P 2024), plus 5G control-channel sniffing that leaks messenger metadata (From 5G Sniffing to Harvesting Leakages, S&P 2023).

The most recent work shown pushes formal rigor into 5G and turns wireless sensing into both a tool and a target. From Control to Chaos (S&P 2025) delivers a comprehensive formal analysis of 5G access control, and Guardians of the Air (S&P 2026) proposes in-device detection of 5G control-plane threats — a defensive answer to the LTE/5G attack lineage that began in 2019. Meanwhile the 2026 cohort reflects where the area now sits: reconfigurable intelligent surfaces and metasurfaces appear on both sides of the fight (The Battle of Metasurfaces; RIS-CLA), WiFi sensing is repurposed for biometric authentication (2FiA), backscatter and LLM guidance enable through-wall keystroke inference (RadKey), jamming becomes physically nonlocalizable (Nonlocalizable Jamming with Curving Beams), and even one-tap conveniences like Google Fast Pair are shown hijackable (One Tap to Hijack Them All). The through-line from 2018 to 2026 is a move from isolated per-protocol breaks toward systematic, formal, and increasingly physics-aware analysis spanning cellular, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, satellite, and RF sensing alike.

ccs.narrative:
Wireless and cellular security at CCS has spanned formal protocol analysis, side-channel attacks over RF, and implementation testing of cellular stacks. A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication (CCS 2018) initiated rigorous scrutiny of 5G protocols before deployment, and 5GReasoner: A Property-Directed Security and Privacy Analysis Framework for 5G Cellular Network Protocol (CCS 2019) extended this to find new cross-layer attacks. Both papers directly influenced 3GPP standardization discussions.

Physical-layer side channels over wireless received landmark treatment: Screaming Channels: When Electromagnetic Side Channels Meet Radio Transceivers (CCS 2018) demonstrated that combined RF transceiver SoCs leak cryptographic key material through their radio antennas, enabling key recovery at distances up to 15 meters. Release the Kraken: New KRACKs in the 802.11 Standard (CCS 2018) found new key-reinstallation vulnerabilities in the WPA2 handshake variants.

Black-box implementation testing matured through 2019-2021: Automatic Fingerprinting of Vulnerable BLE IoT Devices with Static UUIDs from Mobile Apps (CCS 2019) identified BLE device vulnerabilities through companion-app analysis, FirmXRay (CCS 2020) performed static BLE stack analysis in bare-metal firmware, and Noncompliance as Deviant Behavior: An Automated Black-box Noncompliance Checker for 4G LTE Cellular Devices (CCS 2021) automatically discovered noncompliance bugs in commercial 4G phones by black-box testing their control-plane stacks.

milestones.title: A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication
milestones.note: First formal verification of 5G AKA protocol, finding security gaps before widespread 5G deployment.

milestones.note: Discovered that RF transceivers on SoCs emit cryptographic side-channel signals, enabling wireless key extraction.

milestones.note: Found new key-reinstallation attack variants in WPA2 handshake variants not covered by the original KRACK disclosure.

milestones.title: 5GReasoner: A Property-Directed Security and Privacy Analysis Framework for 5G Cellular Network Protocol
milestones.note: Uncovered new cross-layer 5G protocol attacks using property-directed formal reasoning over the full protocol stack.

milestones.note: Extracted static BLE UUIDs from companion apps to fingerprint and rank IoT devices by vulnerability.

milestones.note: Statically analyzed bare-metal BLE firmware to find link-layer vulnerabilities without emulation.

milestones.title: Noncompliance as Deviant Behavior: An Automated Black-box Noncompliance Checker for 4G LTE Cellular Devices
milestones.note: Automatically black-box tested 4G LTE control-plane implementations in commercial phones to find noncompliance bugs.

milestones.note: Crafted robust adversarial perturbations against DNN-based channel estimation in OFDM wireless systems.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list attacks wireless security on two fronts at once. On the cellular side, researchers began treating standards as things to be proven rather than trusted: "A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication" (CCS 2018) ran symbolic verification over the 5G AKA protocol, while "LTEInspector" (NDSS 2018) paired a model checker with a real testbed to systematically hunt for attacks in 4G attach, paging, and detach procedures. Alongside these protocol analyses came sharply physical attacks — "Screaming Channels" (CCS 2018) leaked crypto secrets through a chip's own radio, "All Your GPS Are Belong To Us" (USENIX 2018) quietly steered drivers off course, and "Release the Kraken" (CCS 2018) extended the KRACK weaknesses in the 802.11 standard. Even privacy leaks were structural, as "GUTI Reallocation Demystified" (NDSS 2018) showed temporary cellular identifiers could still track users.

2019 and 2020 turned these openings into a wave of concrete, mostly implementation-level breaks. Cellular research matured fast: "Breaking LTE on Layer Two" (S&P 2019) exploited unauthenticated layer-two framing, "Touching the Untouchables" (S&P 2019) and "5GReasoner" (CCS 2019) pushed dynamic and property-directed analysis of the control plane, "Hiding in Plain Signal" (USENIX 2019) overshadowed legitimate LTE signals, and "IMP4GT" (NDSS 2020) achieved full impersonation in 4G. The same period cracked short-range radio: "The KNOB is Broken" (USENIX 2019) and "BIAS" (S&P 2020) undermined Bluetooth key negotiation and authentication at the standard level, while "Dragonblood" (S&P 2020) broke WPA3's brand-new Dragonfly handshake. A recurring theme emerges — formal and side-channel methods from one venue keep feeding attacks demonstrated at another.

From 2020 onward the field pivoted from protocol logic to the messy reality of firmware and expanded to every RF surface in sight. "Frankenstein" (USENIX 2020) and "FirmXRay" (CCS 2020) fuzzed and statically audited Bluetooth firmware, and "FirmWire" (NDSS 2022) made cellular baseband firmware transparently analyzable at scale — a decisive shift from modeling protocols to executing the code that implements them. Meanwhile the target list broadened well past phones and laptops: maritime VSAT links ("A Tale of Sea and Sky", S&P 2020), automotive OBD-II dongles ("Plug-N-Pwned", USENIX 2020), UAVs under GPS spoofing (USENIX 2022), adversarial physical-layer sensing ("IRShield", S&P 2022), and even satellites ("Space Odyssey", S&P 2023).

The most recent work, clustered in NDSS 2026, shows a field that is simultaneously deepening its rigor and chasing new attack surfaces. Formal methods and semantic fuzzing now target Bluetooth Low Energy directly — "Formal Analysis of BLE Secure Connection Pairing" reveals a new PE Confusion attack, "BLERP" breaks BLE re-pairing, and "BSFuzzer" hunts BLE logic flaws — while "WCDCAnalyzer" brings scalable analysis to Wi-Fi device-connectivity protocols. Classic cellular threats persist and evolve, with "Passive Multi-Target GUTI Identification via Visual-RF Correlation" and "Small Cell, Big Risk" auditing LTE femtocells in the wild, and entirely new vectors appear, from "XR Devices Send WiFi Packets When They Should Not" enabling cross-building keylogging to "SIPConfusion" spoofing caller ID and attacks on aircraft collision-avoidance (TCAS). The through-line from 2018 holds: rigorous analysis of protocols and their implementations, now applied to an ever-wider universe of wireless devices.
